question: Did learned positional embeddings beat sinusoidal positional encodings in the Transformer experiments, and why did the authors keep the sinusoidal version?
answer: 3.5 Positional Encoding Since our model contains no recurrence and no convolution, in order for the model to make use of the order of the sequence, we must inject some information about the relative or absolute position of the tokens in the sequence [Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, p. 6, Section 3.5 Positional Encoding]. To this end, we add "positional encodings" to the input embeddings at the bottoms of the encoder and decoder stacks [Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, p. 6, Section 3.5 Positional Encoding]. The positional encodings have the same dimension dmodel as the embeddings, so that the two can be summed [Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, p. 6, Section 3.5 Positional Encoding]. There are many choices of positional encodings, learned and fixed [9] [Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, p. 6, Section 3.5 Positional Encoding]. In this work, we use sine and cosine functions of different frequencies: PE(pos,2i) = sin(pos/100002i/dmodel) PE(pos,2i+1) = cos(pos/100002i/dmodel) where pos is the position and i is the dimension [Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, p. 6, Section 3.5 Positional Encoding].

question: Which dataset gave Moshi its full-duplex ability, and what property of that dataset made it suitable?
Which dataset gave Moshi its full-duplex ability, and what property of that dataset made it suitable?
answer: The only previous full-duplex dialogue system is dGSLM (Nguyen et al., 2023), which models user and system speech as separate audio token streams and proposes a Siamese architecture to process both streams jointly [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, arXiv:2410.00037v1, p. 6, Section 2 Related Work]. While dGSLM is full-duplex, it remains a proof-of-concept: it does not run in an online fashion, it does not benefit from the knowledge of a text language model, and it does not model acoustic information as it only models semantic tokens [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, arXiv:2410.00037v1, p. 6, Section 2 Related Work]. Moshi addresses these limitations altogether: by modeling two streams of semantic and acoustic tokens hierarchically, Moshi is full duplex and can exploit all the information from the user (linguistic and non-linguistic) while producing speech in real time [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, arXiv:2410.00037v1, p. 6, Section 2 Related Work]. Thanks to text pretraining and Inner Monologue, Moshi benefits from the knowledge of its Helium backbone [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, arXiv:2410.00037v1, p. 6, Section 2 Related Work]. Finally, as the model produces acoustic tokens along with text and semantic tokens, it can generate an arbitrary range of emotions, voices and acoustic conditions [Moshi: a speech-text foundation model for real-time dialogue, arXiv:2410.00037v1, p. 6, Section 2 Related Work].
answer_raw: The only previous full-duplex dialogue system is dGSLM (Nguyen et al., 2023), which models user and system speech as separate audio token streams and proposes a Siamese architecture to process both streams jointly [P1]. While dGSLM is full-duplex, it remains a proof-of-concept: it does not run in an online fashion, it does not benefit from the knowledge of a text language model, and it does not model acoustic information as it only models semantic tokens [P1]. Moshi addresses these limitations altogether: by modeling two streams of semantic and acoustic tokens hierarchically, Moshi is full duplex and can exploit all the information from the user (linguistic and non-linguistic) while producing speech in real time [P1]. Thanks to text pretraining and Inner Monologue, Moshi benefits from the knowledge of its Helium backbone [P1]. Finally, as the model produces acoustic tokens along with text and semantic tokens, it can generate an arbitrary range of emotions, voices and acoustic conditions [P1].

question: Moshi and H-Net both describe hierarchical models. What does each level of the hierarchy operate over in each paper?
Why does scaled dot-product attention divide the dot products by the square root of d_k?
answer: 3.2.1 Scaled Dot-Product Attention We call our particular attention "Scaled Dot-Product Attention" (Figure 2) [Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, p. 4, Section 3.2.1 Scaled Dot-Product Attention]. The input consists of queries and keys of dimension dk, and values of dimension dv [Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, p. 4, Section 3.2.1 Scaled Dot-Product Attention]. We compute the dot products of the query with all keys, divide each by √dk, and apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the values [Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, p. 4, Section 3.2.1 Scaled Dot-Product Attention]. In practice, we compute the attention function on a set of queries simultaneously, packed together into a matrix Q [Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, p. 4, Section 3.2.1 Scaled Dot-Product Attention]. The keys and values are also packed together into matrices K and V  [Attention Is All You Need, arXiv:1706.03762v7, p. 4, Section 3.2.1 Scaled Dot-Product Attention].
answer_raw: 3.2.1 Scaled Dot-Product Attention We call our particular attention "Scaled Dot-Product Attention" (Figure 2) [P1]. The input consists of queries and keys of dimension dk, and values of dimension dv [P1]. We compute the dot products of the query with all keys, divide each by √dk, and apply a softmax function to obtain the weights on the values [P1]. In practice, we compute the attention function on a set of queries simultaneously, packed together into a matrix Q [P1]. The keys and values are also packed together into matrices K and V  [P1].
